parts: Lesson 20: Sectoral Aspects of Indian Economy — Summary

We use food items (cereals, pulses, fruit, oil) produced by farmers in villages, and non-food items (clothes, shoes, furniture, vehicles) produced by industries in towns and cities. The occupations people follow are grouped into three sectors.

The primary sector covers (1) agriculture and allied activities such as livestock, poultry and dairy, (2) fishery, (3) forestry — timber, firewood and herbal medicines — and (4) mining and quarrying. These are the traditional rural occupations, and crops give both food and non-food items such as cotton and jute.

Towns and cities are urban areas, such as Jaipur, Pune and Bhubaneswar. Delhi, Chennai, Mumbai and Kolkata are metros. Urban areas are known for non-agricultural activities in the secondary and tertiary sectors.
The secondary sector covers three activities.
(1) Manufacturing makes goods from raw materials in factories. Small-scale examples are shoes, textiles, printing, glass and furniture; large-scale examples are steel, automobiles and aluminium.
(2) Construction builds houses, roads, bridges, dams and airports. It is a regular activity in both rural and urban areas.

The service sector includes trade, hotels and restaurants; transport, storage and communication; finance (banking and insurance); real estate and business services; public administration; and other services.
In 2009–10, about 50% of workers were in agriculture, 13.3% in manufacturing and 13.2% in trade and hotels.
(1) Share in national income: more than 50% at independence, about 15% in 2009–10.
(2) Employment: it is the largest employer. About 70% of people depended on it at independence and about 50% in 2009–10.
(3) Food for millions: food-grain output was about 234 million tonnes in 2008–09.
(4) Raw materials for industry: sugar, jute, cotton textiles, vanaspati, paper (from grass and bamboo) and food processing (pickles, jam, juice, biscuits).

A small-scale industry needs at least ₹25 lakh of spending on plant and machinery and is mostly labour-intensive. Large-scale industry needs huge capital investment and is capital-intensive, e.g. Tata Steel at Jamshedpur.
(1) Share in national income: 14% at independence, 28% in 2009–10.
(2) Employment: about 3.3 crore people work in industry, about 3.12 crore of them in small industries.
(3) Infrastructure: roads, railways, dams (Hirakud, Bhakra-Nangal), buildings and communication towers.
(4) Consumer goods such as clothes, pens, soap, cycles and cars.
Small industries help nation-building, and self-employed people run their own small businesses.
(1) National income: the largest share, 55.2% in 2009–10.
(2) Employment: 29.4% of workers. It pays more than agriculture and offers year-round, non-seasonal work, so educated people move to it.
(3) Foreign funds: banking, insurance, trade, transport, hotels and computer services attract foreign direct investment, which creates jobs.
(4) Exports: IT, consultancy and legal services earned about ₹4.35 lakh crore in 2009–10.

The sectors support each other. Industry supplies farmers with pumps, fertiliser and tractors, and agriculture supplies food and raw materials to industry. Services — transport (trucks), communication (mobile phones), banking (cheques) and trade (shops) — make these exchanges possible. The farmer Hari Singh sells wheat, buys a diesel pump through a hardware shop, and the same truck carries food back to the industrial town.
